title: Equity Beyond Bias in Language Technologies for Education
venue: Proceedings of the Fourteenth Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications
extended_summary:
This paper argues that work on fairness in educational language technologies must move beyond narrow notions of model bias and allocational harm to address broader equity concerns. The authors synthesize literature from fair machine learning, sociocultural and critical pedagogy, and education research to propose a roadmap for designing, evaluating, and implementing NLP systems in education in ways that support equity rather than reproduce existing inequalities.

Rather than reporting a single empirical intervention, the paper develops a conceptual agenda and applies it through case studies across several educational NLP domains, including intelligent tutoring systems, reading comprehension, automated writing feedback and scoring, computer-assisted language learning, and student engagement/sentiment analysis. Across these examples, it highlights how representational harms, linguistic imperialism, surveillance, and culturally misaligned assessments can disadvantage students from marginalized racial, linguistic, cultural, and gender groups.

The paper concludes that equitable educational technology requires culturally competent development teams, intentional representation in system design, transparent and accountable deployment, and attention to what problems should not be solved by automation at all. It emphasizes that educational NLP can support learning and assessment, but only if systems are built with local context, student identity, and power relations in mind.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed workshop position/review paper, not an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature and offers recommendations, but it does not report original study design, causal identification, or new outcome data.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has meaningful conceptual impact for equity-oriented educational AI governance and design, especially around subgroup risks and tradeoffs, but it does not demonstrate measured intervention effects. Its practical influence is likely broader than its empirical evidence base, yet the direct educational impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Discusses agent-based intelligent tutoring systems that use human-like text or speech agents, including avatar/pedagogical agent design, culturally congruent representation, and scaffolding in reading comprehension and other educational interactions.

Reviews NLP-based tools for automated essay scoring, grammar/error correction, readability assessment, text simplification, and computer-assisted language learning feedback for writing and language practice.
Covers automated scoring and formative feedback systems for student writing, including rubric-based feedback, rhetorical structure feedback, and automated assessment of essays.
Mentions speech-enabled and NLP-based instructional systems for reading comprehension questions, vocabulary practice, pronunciation training, and other software-delivered learning tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that NLP tools in reading comprehension and writing can support literacy, but they often privilege factoid assessment, dominant cultural norms, and rigid rubrics. It cites prior work showing improved outcomes for culturally congruent educational technologies and embodied tutors, but also warns that question generation and automated scoring may under-measure growth for students of color and nonstandard language users; no new effect size is reported because this is a conceptual review.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension quality, writing assessment quality, and culturally responsive literacy support

finding.finding_summary: For computer-assisted language learning and speech technologies, the paper presents the literature as generally effective for vocabulary building, pronunciation training, and language practice, while emphasizing equity risks for dialect speakers and multilingual learners. It highlights that systems can fail to recognize marginalized dialects or support code-switching, but no single quantitative effect estimate is reported in this review.
finding.measure: Pronunciation/vocabulary practice, speech recognition performance, and support for multilingual/dialect variation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that always-on sentiment, affect, and engagement monitoring may increase anxiety, paranoia, and behavior gaming, especially when students know they are being observed. It also notes that affect-aware tutoring and socioemotional interventions are promising, but warns of discriminatory outcomes by gender, race, and age; no pooled effect size is given in this position paper.
finding.measure: Student anxiety, perceived surveillance, affect recognition outcomes, and engagement monitoring

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames culturally responsive NLP tools as potentially supporting dialogue, critical discourse, and student agency, but criticizes factoid-oriented systems for failing to promote deeper thinking. It emphasizes that reading and writing tools should support critical thinking and dialogue rather than only surface accuracy; no new quantitative estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, dialogue, and culturally responsive participation

finding.finding_summary: This is primarily an equity-and-governance paper arguing that educational NLP can both reduce and reproduce institutional harms through representation, surveillance, and linguistic imperialism. It does not present new experimental data, but synthesizes prior evidence that biased models, privacy-invasive monitoring, and culturally narrow designs can produce disparate outcomes across race, gender, age, and language groups.
finding.measure: Equity, bias, privacy/control, and institutional harms in educational AI systems
